explication:
<explanation>
1. Project Type and Purpose  
   - This is a static content website built with Jekyll (Ruby) that hosts an “Awesome ChatGPT Prompts” collection.  
   - It uses GitHub as the source repository, GitHub Actions for CI/CD, and GitHub Pages (and related services like prompts.chat and Hugging Face) for hosting.

2. File Structure Analysis  
   - Top level:  
     • `.github/workflows/` – CI pipelines (linting, publishing).  
     • `_config.yml`, `_layouts/` – Jekyll configuration and HTML templates.  
     • `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `LICENSE` – documentation.  
     • `Gemfile` – Ruby dependencies for Jekyll.  
     • `scripts/` – auxiliary command-line tools (e.g., `find-prompt`).  
     • Static assets: `style.css`, `script.js`, `vibe/` sub-site, CSV data files.  
   - Key patterns:  
     • SSG (Static Site Generator) architecture  
     • Content → Jekyll → HTML/CSS/JS → deploy  
     • CI/CD pipelines trigger on push/PR to build and publish  

3. README Insights  
   - Describes site purpose (curated prompts), external links (prompts.chat, Hugging Face).  
   - Mentions badges, sponsor logos, unmerged PRs.  
   - No backend/API; everything is pre-rendered static content.

4. System Design Diagram Guidelines  
   a. Main Components  
      - Developer workstation (local clone + Jekyll CLI)  
      - Source repository (GitHub)  
      - GitHub Actions CI pipelines (build, lint, publish)  
      - Jekyll engine (build step)  
      - Output artifacts (static HTML/CSS/JS)  
      - Hosting layer (GitHub Pages, CDN)  
      - External services (prompts.chat mirror, Hugging Face dataset)  
   b. Relationships & Data Flow  
      1. Developer edits Markdown, configs, scripts locally.  
      2. Push to GitHub → triggers Actions workflows.  
      3. CI installs gems, runs Jekyll build → produces `_site` directory.  
      4. CI publishes `_site` to `gh-pages` branch or Pages environment.  
      5. GitHub Pages (and CDN) serves static site to end users.  
      6. External mirrors (prompts.chat, Hugging Face) pull or sync content.  
   c. Architectural Patterns  
      - Static Site Generator with “build once, serve many” principle  
      - GitOps / CI-driven deployment  
      - Content/manuscript separation via `_layouts` and Markdown  
   d. Core Technologies  
      - Jekyll (Ruby), Liquid templates  
      - GitHub Actions (YAML workflows)  
      - GitHub Pages, CDN  
      - Vanilla JS / CSS for interactivity and styling  
      - Custom scripts in `scripts/` for content tooling  

5. Tailoring the Diagram for a Static Site  
   - Emphasize the build pipeline: local → GitHub → Actions → build → deploy  
   - Show repository branches (e.g., `main`, `gh-pages`) and workflow triggers  
   - Highlight the absence of runtime servers or databases  
   - If desired, include how sponsors and external badges (Graphite, Warp, Clemta) are embedded as external assets  

6. Diagramming Best Practices  
   - Components as rounded rectangles or grouped swimlanes (Dev, CI, Hosting, External)  
   - Directional arrows for push/pull and build/deploy flows  
   - Color coding:  
     • Blue for developer/dev-tools  
     • Green for CI/CD  
     • Orange for hosting/CDN  
     • Gray for external mirrors/services  
   - Clear labels: name each step (e.g., “Jekyll Build,” “Publish to Pages”)  
   - Legend or key for color and shape semantics  

7. “More Beautiful” Enhancements  
   - Use icons (GitHub logo, Jekyll icon, cloud/CDN symbol)  
   - Apply a clean layout with left-to-right flow  
   - Group related elements in lightly shaded containers (e.g., CI workflows)  
   - Annotate timing or triggers (e.g., “on push to main”) with small callouts  
   - Optionally overlay a simple sequence numbering to guide viewers  

By following these steps and styling suggestions, the resulting diagram will be both accurate and visually pleasing, clearly reflecting this Jekyll-powered, GitHub-driven static site architecture.  
</explanation>
